title: Aware But Undecided: What the GAO Found the United States Knew About the Peso in 1994
participants: Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público
House Committee on Banking and Financial Services

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim was the yield on the instrument. Tesobonos were short-dated Mexican government paper indexed to the dollar, so foreign holders "were spared the" exchange risk and accepted "lower interest rates for tesobonos than for cetes" — on 20 April 1994 the 91-day tesobono rate was 6.6 percent. Cheap funding for the issuer, no currency risk for the buyer, and the risk relocated entirely into the reserve position that would have to honour it.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the switch, and GAO dates it: "on the last week of April, there was nearly a sevenfold increase in tesobonos", and over 1994 tesobonos went "from 6.4 percent to 70.2 percent of total foreign investment" in Mexican securities. A current account deficit financed by short-term dollar-linked obligations, which GAO notes "forestalled" the pressure rather than relieving it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is in the sequencing of who learned what. Through 1994 US officials monitored the peso and were "aware that Mexico was experiencing a large current account deficit financed mostly by short-term portfolio capital that was vulnerable to a sudden reversal of investor confidence"; a Treasury official felt "even in February 1994" that the rate was "on the high side"; the Federal Reserve had been concerned "even before 1994". The market learned later and all at once: "As investors became aware that Mexico had only about $6 billion in foreign reserves in early January 1995, they were increasingly concerned about the possibility of default and sought to redeem their investments."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The backstop was the largest of its kind to that date: "a financial assistance package of up to $48.8 billion" from the United States, Canada, the IMF and the BIS, of which the United States pledged "up to $20 billion in loans and securities guarantees from ESF", the Exchange Stabilization Fund, with the Federal Reserve providing "up to $6 billion in short-term swaps from its preexisting swap line". Who the money ultimately paid is the contested question, and GAO records the objection without adopting it.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The containment is in GAO's own scoping, stated as a limit rather than concealed: GAO "did not address the issue of whether Mexico would be able to repay the United States for the assistance". The report examines awareness, authority and terms. It does not audit the outcome, and this dossier does not pretend otherwise.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The Exchange Stabilization Fund and a pre-existing Federal Reserve swap line with Mexico — standing facilities that could be drawn without new legislation, which is why GAO was asked to analyse "the statutory authority for the Secretary of the Treasury's use of the Exchange Stabilization Fund" after the fact rather than before.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A $48.8 billion multilateral template for rescuing a sovereign's short-term debt stock, and a congressional record arguing about it — the objection that "tesobono investors should not have been shielded from financial losses" and that shielding them "could make future Mexico-like crises more likely" is preserved in a GAO report to a House committee.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A dollar-indexed instrument removes currency risk from the buyer and concentrates it in the reserve; the reserve is drawn down defending the peg; the smaller reserve makes the obligations less credible; the less credible obligations shorten still further, until $12.5 billion of reserves faces $30 billion of maturities and only an official creditor can clear the gap.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That Washington knew the peso was going to break, said nothing, and then used $20 billion of public money to make Wall Street's tesobono holders whole.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The report that the viral account relies on is the one that refuses it, and it does so in the same paragraph as the concession. GAO found US officials were aware of the structural vulnerability, that a senior Treasury official thought the rate "on the high side" in February 1994, that the Federal Reserve had been concerned even earlier, and that in October and November "high-level U.S. officials cautioned Mexican officials that the peso seemed overvalued". Then: "U.S. officials, however, were undecided about the extent to which the peso was overvalued and if and when financial markets might force Mexico to take action. Moreover, Federal Reserve and Treasury officials did not foresee the magnitude of the crisis that eventually unfolded." And a detail that is hard for any insider-knowledge account to absorb: swap facilities were "made ... potentially available" in March and August 1994 and "Mexico did not use these facilities during this period" — the lines were open and undrawn before the break. GAO also records that the IMF "was less aware of the seriousness of the situation" than the US government, which is the opposite of a coordinated operation. The bailed-out-bondholders argument is not absent from the report: it is there, attributed — "Some observers opposed any U.S. financial assistance ... They argued that tesobono investors should not have been shielded from financial losses" — as a position held by critics, not as a finding. What the record supports is an asymmetry of attention rather than of plot: officials holding a correct general worry they could not time, against a market that did not price the reserve position until January 1995.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: GAO/GGD-96-56, a report of 23 February 1996 to the Chairman of the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services, whose stated purpose includes assessing "the extent to which the U.S. government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) were aware of Mexico's financial problems throughout 1994". It records: reserves fallen to $12.5 billion against $30 billion of tesobono obligations maturing in 1995; a nearly sevenfold increase in tesobonos in the last week of April 1994 and a rise from 6.4 to 70.2 percent of total foreign investment in Mexican securities; a 91-day tesobono rate of 6.6 percent on 20 April 1994; US officials aware through 1994 of a current account deficit financed by short-term portfolio capital vulnerable to sudden reversal; a Treasury memorandum on the inflation differential and an official who thought the rate "on the high side" in February 1994; Federal Reserve concern predating 1994; two large swap facilities made potentially available in March and August 1994 and not used; high-level cautions to Mexican officials in October and November; officials nonetheless undecided on the extent of overvaluation and timing, and not foreseeing the magnitude of the crisis; the IMF less aware than the US government and seeing no compelling case for a change in exchange rate policy for most of 1994; about $10 billion of tesobonos due in the three months from January 1995 against about $6 billion of reserves, which investors became aware of in early January 1995; and an assistance package of up to $48.8 billion, including up to $20 billion of US loans and guarantees from the Exchange Stabilization Fund and up to $6 billion of Federal Reserve swaps. GAO expressly did not address whether Mexico would repay.

citations.title: U.S. General Accounting Office, "Mexico's Financial Crisis: Origins, Awareness, Assistance, and Initial Efforts to Recover", GAO/GGD-96-56, report to the Chairman, Committee on Banking and Financial Services, House of Representatives, 23 February 1996
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from gao.gov (784 KB) and read as extracted text. (gao.gov refuses a generic automated request with HTTP 403 and serves the file to a request declaring an identity and contact address, so automated link checks report this URL as blocked rather than dead.) The report exists to answer the advance-knowledge question directly: it was asked to assess "the extent to which the U.S. government and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) were aware of Mexico's financial problems throughout 1994 and provided advice to Mexico", and "Awareness" is a word in its title. THE POSITION AT THE BREAK: Mexico "became vulnerable to a financial market crisis because its foreign exchange reserves had fallen to $12.5 billion while it had tesobono obligations of $30 billion maturing in 1995". Tesobonos were short-term dollar-indexed Mexican government paper; "on the last week of April" 1994 "there was nearly a sevenfold increase in tesobonos", and tesobonos rose "from 6.4 percent to 70.2 percent of total foreign investment" in Mexican securities. WHAT THE UNITED STATES KNEW, IN GAO'S WORDS: "Throughout 1994, the U.S. government monitored economic and political developments that affected the value of Mexico's peso. In early 1994, U.S. officials had some concerns over the sustainability of Mexico's exchange rate policies in the short run. They were aware that Mexico was experiencing a large current account deficit financed mostly by short-term portfolio capital that was vulnerable to a sudden reversal of investor confidence in Mexico." A Treasury memorandum is recorded as expressing concern about the inflation differential; a senior Treasury official told GAO that "even in February 1994 he felt that Mexico's exchange rate was 'on the high side'"; and "A Federal Reserve official told us that the Federal Reserve had become concerned about the size of Mexico's current account deficit and its exchange rate policy even before 1994." WHAT THEY DID WITH IT: "During March and August, the Federal Reserve and Treasury made two large swap facilities potentially available to Mexico" — "Mexico did not use these facilities during this period" — and "During October and November, high-level U.S. officials cautioned Mexican officials that the peso seemed overvalued and indicated that it was risky to continue the existing exchange rate policy." AND THE LIMIT GAO PUTS ON ALL OF IT, which is the sentence this dossier is built around: "U.S. officials, however, were undecided about the extent to which the peso was overvalued and if and when financial markets might force Mexico to take action. Moreover, Federal Reserve and Treasury officials did not foresee the magnitude of the crisis that eventually unfolded. IMF was less aware of the seriousness of the situation that was developing in Mexico during 1994 than was the U.S. government and, for most of 1994, did not see a compelling case for a change in Mexico's exchange rate policy." GAO also records that these concerns "were outweighed by a number of other considerations that pointed to a more optimistic view", including the belief that Mexico "had sound economic fundamentals" after a decade of reform. WHO LEARNED WHAT, AND WHEN, IN JANUARY 1995: "In January 1995, Mexico faced the need to pay out about $10 billion for tesobonos coming due in the following 3 months unless it could convince bondholders to buy new Mexican government debt securities. As investors became aware that Mexico had only about $6 billion in foreign reserves in early January 1995, they were increasingly concerned about the possibility of default and sought to redeem their investments." THE PACKAGE: "a financial assistance package of up to $48.8 billion in funds from the United States, Canada, the International Monetary Fund (IMF), and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS)", of which "The United States pledged up to $20 billion in loans and securities guarantees from ESF" — the Exchange Stabilization Fund — "As part of the amount, the Federal Reserve agreed to provide up to $6 billion in short-term swaps from its preexisting swap line." THE BAILED-OUT-BONDHOLDERS ARGUMENT IS IN THE REPORT, ATTRIBUTED, NOT ADOPTED: "Some observers opposed any U.S. financial assistance to Mexico. They argued that tesobono investors should not have been shielded from financial losses, and that neither the danger posed by the spread of Mexico's crisis to other nations nor the risk to U.S. trade, employment, and immigration were sufficient to justify such assistance." GAO expressly "did not address the issue of whether Mexico would be able to repay the United States for the assistance."
